title: Canonical resumable handoff: AsyncIterator <-> ReadableStream adapter with mid-stream checkpoints
creator: Aisha Rahman
description:
Problem: Customers integrate Redwood's streaming responses into heterogeneous runtimes and UIs. We currently provide separate helpers for AsyncIterator and Web ReadableStream consumption, but real applications need to: 1) switch a consumer mid-run (handoff) without losing tokens, 2) resume a partially-consumed stream after a transient error, and 3) preserve backpressure semantics when bridging between async iterator and Web Streams.

Goals:
- Design a canonical adapter API in the TypeScript SDK that supports: graceful consumer handoff, mid-stream checkpointing (KV-cache-like token offsets), and resumption across network retries.
- Provide a compact ergonomic surface: a single adapter that exposes both an AsyncIterator and a ReadableStream and supports pause/resume and safe forking (tee) semantics where possible.
- Maintain strong TypeScript types and minimal bundle impact.
- Document examples and migration guide for customers using older stream helpers.

Acceptance criteria:
- API implemented in ts-sdk core exposing createResumableStream(responseStream, options) -> { asyncIterator, readableStream, checkpoint, resume }
- Backpressure is preserved in common scenarios (for-await consumer, ReadableStream.getReader consumer) per benchmark tests.
- Unit + integration tests simulating consumer handoff, network interruption with resume token, and concurrent tee/readers.
- PR with docs/examples and a short migration note.
- Benchmarked overhead < 5% in median throughput compared to raw streaming consumer for 1k token responses.

Non-goals:
- Not adding server-side checkpoint tokens (we'll use local offsets/byte cursors for now).
- Not changing runtime streaming protocol (SSE/WebSocket).
comments: 2026-03-10 - Aisha Rahman: Created ticket after Friday WG where multiple customers asked for resumable streaming for mobile SDKs. Initial design sketch attached below. Marking P0 because this blocks one enterprise pilot that must support flaky mobile networks.

2026-03-11 - Ethan Liu: Spike complete. Implemented prototype adapter that tees an incoming ReadableStream to two sinks and tracks last-complete-chunk index. Prototype link: https://github.com/redwood-inference/redwood-sdk/compare/stream-resume-spike. Observed that naive tee loses backpressure in Node 18 fetch polyfill; need explicit pull controller bridging layer.

2026-03-11 - Ethan Liu: Decision: implement a 'pull-through' ReadableStream that consumes the low-level byte stream and exposes an AsyncIterator wrapper backed by an internal queue with high-water and low-water marks for backpressure. Keep the internal queue scalar (string chunks) to avoid heavy copying.
Follow-ups: add ABI for checkpoint metadata (sequence number + lastByteOffset) so callers can persist minimal state.

2026-03-12 - PM review (Lina Gomez): Confirming API ergonomics are important for PLG users. Please include migration snippet for customers using for await (stream) => { } and those using response.body.getReader().read().

2026-03-12 - Design (Marco Tan): UX note: example should show 'handoff' pattern where UI swaps from server-render to client-render consumer without duplicate tokens or double-counting costs. We'll add a snippet in the docs showing 'teeToClientAndCache' helper.
notes: Key engineering challenges: Node fetch polyfill differences, maintaining zero-copy where possible for large token payloads, ensuring that resume semantics are deterministic across retries. Plan to add a small opt-in persistence layer example that writes checkpoint metadata to IndexedDB for web clients and to local file / secure store in mobile clients.
